title: Microbial Morphology & Physiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Microbial Morphology & Physiology curriculum: detailed prokaryotic cell ultrastructure (wall, membrane, cytoplasmic components, appendages, endospores), microbial nutrition and metabolism, growth kinetics, and the physical/chemical factors that govern microbial growth -- builds on the introductory survey in General Microbiology I without repeating it.

questions.question: The rigidity of the bacterial cell wall is primarily due to a polymer called:
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan (murein) is a mesh-like polymer of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid cross-linked by peptide bridges that gives the bacterial cell wall its rigidity and shape.

questions.question: Which structural feature accounts for Gram-negative bacteria staining pink/red after the Gram stain procedure?
options: A thin peptidoglycan layer that allows the crystal violet-iodine complex to be washed out by decolouriser, revealing the safranin counterstain
A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps the crystal violet-iodine complex
Absence of a cell wall altogether
The presence of chitin in place of peptidoglycan
questions.correct_answer: A thin peptidoglycan layer that allows the crystal violet-iodine complex to be washed out by decolouriser, revealing the safranin counterstain
questions.explanation: Gram-negative cells have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane; the decolouriser disrupts the outer membrane and washes out the crystal violet-iodine complex, so the cells take up the safranin counterstain.

questions.question: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which acts as an endotoxin, is a component of the:
questions.explanation: LPS is embedded in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria; its lipid A portion is the endotoxin responsible for fever and septic shock.

questions.question: Teichoic acids are characteristic components found in the cell wall of:
questions.explanation: Teichoic acids are anionic polymers woven through the thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria, contributing to wall rigidity and adhesion.

questions.question: The bacterial cytoplasmic membrane is best described chemically as a:
questions.explanation: Like other biological membranes, the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer studded with integral and peripheral proteins that carry out transport, respiration, and signalling.

questions.question: In bacteria, oxidative phosphorylation (the electron transport chain) occurs across the:
questions.explanation: Bacteria lack mitochondria, so the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located in the cytoplasmic membrane, which functions analogously to the mitochondrial inner membrane.

questions.question: The region of a bacterial cell containing the single circular chromosome, which is not bound by a membrane, is called the:
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes and lack a true membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA is condensed into an irregular region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid.

questions.question: Bacterial ribosomes have a sedimentation coefficient of:
questions.explanation: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, composed of 30S and 50S subunits, distinguishing them from the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotic cytoplasm -- the basis of selective toxicity for several antibiotics.

questions.question: Small extrachromosomal, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that often carry antibiotic-resistance genes in bacteria are called:
questions.explanation: Plasmids are self-replicating extrachromosomal DNA elements that are not essential for survival but often confer selective advantages such as antibiotic resistance.

questions.question: Bacterial cytoplasmic inclusion bodies such as polyhydroxybutyrate granules and volutin (metachromatic) granules mainly function as:
options: Storage reserves of carbon, energy or phosphate
questions.correct_answer: Storage reserves of carbon, energy or phosphate
questions.explanation: Inclusion bodies store nutrients (carbon/energy polymers, phosphate, sulfur) that the cell can mobilise when external nutrients become scarce.

questions.question: The gelatinous, well-organised layer that surrounds some bacterial cells and is firmly attached to the cell wall, often contributing to virulence, is called the:
questions.explanation: A capsule is a discrete, well-defined polysaccharide (or polypeptide) layer firmly attached to the cell wall that helps bacteria resist phagocytosis and desiccation.

questions.question: Compared to a capsule, a slime layer differs mainly in that it is:
options: Loosely attached and diffuse rather than tightly organised
Composed of protein rather than polysaccharide
questions.correct_answer: Loosely attached and diffuse rather than tightly organised
questions.explanation: A slime layer is a diffuse, unorganised, loosely attached extracellular substance, whereas a capsule is thicker and more tightly and discretely bound to the cell surface.

questions.question: Bacterial flagella are primarily responsible for:
questions.explanation: Flagella are helical protein filaments rotated by a motor embedded in the cell envelope, propelling the bacterium through liquid media.

questions.question: A bacterium with a single flagellum located at one pole of the cell is described as:
questions.explanation: Monotrichous flagellar arrangement refers to a single flagellum at one pole, as seen in Vibrio cholerae; peritrichous means flagella distributed over the entire surface, as in E. coli.

questions.question: Pili (fimbriae) differ from flagella chiefly in that pili are:
options: Shorter, thinner, non-motile appendages used for attachment or DNA transfer
Longer structures used exclusively for swimming
Made of peptidoglycan rather than protein
questions.correct_answer: Shorter, thinner, non-motile appendages used for attachment or DNA transfer
questions.explanation: Pili are short, hair-like proteinaceous appendages used for adherence to surfaces (common pili) or for conjugative DNA transfer (sex pilus), unlike flagella which drive motility.

questions.question: Bacterial endospores are primarily a survival mechanism produced in response to:
options: Nutrient depletion or unfavourable environmental conditions
questions.correct_answer: Nutrient depletion or unfavourable environmental conditions
questions.explanation: Sporulation is triggered mainly by nutrient starvation, allowing genera such as Bacillus and Clostridium to form dormant, highly resistant endospores that survive harsh conditions.

questions.question: The heat resistance of bacterial endospores is largely attributed to:
options: Dipicolinic acid complexed with calcium in the spore core
A thick capsule surrounding the spore
High water content of the spore core
The presence of flagella on the spore
questions.correct_answer: Dipicolinic acid complexed with calcium in the spore core
questions.explanation: Calcium-dipicolinate stabilises spore DNA and proteins and, together with the spore's very low water content, confers exceptional resistance to heat, radiation and chemicals.

questions.question: The process by which a dormant endospore returns to active vegetative growth is called:
questions.explanation: Germination is the process in which a spore, triggered by favourable conditions, sheds its resistant properties and re-enters vegetative growth; sporulation is the reverse process of spore formation.

questions.question: Organisms that obtain both carbon and energy from organic compounds are nutritionally classified as:
questions.explanation: Chemoheterotrophs use organic compounds as both their carbon source and their energy source; most bacteria, fungi and all animals fall into this category.

questions.question: An organism that uses light as its energy source and carbon dioxide as its carbon source is a:
questions.explanation: Photoautotrophs, such as cyanobacteria, derive energy from light (photo-) and carbon from CO2 fixation (-autotroph), similarly to plants.

questions.question: Chemoautotrophic bacteria such as nitrifying bacteria obtain energy by:
questions.explanation: Chemoautotrophs (chemolithotrophs) gain energy by oxidising inorganic substrates such as ammonia, nitrite, sulfur or iron, while fixing CO2 as their carbon source.

questions.question: During the lag phase of a bacterial growth curve, the cells are mainly:
options: Synthesising enzymes and adapting metabolically to the new environment with little increase in cell number
Dividing at the maximum possible rate
Dying off rapidly due to nutrient exhaustion
questions.correct_answer: Synthesising enzymes and adapting metabolically to the new environment with little increase in cell number
questions.explanation: In the lag phase, cells are metabolically active, synthesising enzymes and macromolecules needed for growth in the new medium, but cell numbers increase little, if at all.

questions.question: The phase of the bacterial growth curve during which cell number increases exponentially at a constant maximum rate is the:
questions.explanation: In the log phase, cells divide at a constant maximal rate by binary fission, and the population doubles at regular intervals (the generation time), producing exponential growth.

questions.question: The stationary phase of bacterial growth occurs mainly because:
options: The rate of new cell formation equals the rate of cell death, often due to nutrient depletion and waste accumulation
Cells begin dividing faster than in the log phase
questions.correct_answer: The rate of new cell formation equals the rate of cell death, often due to nutrient depletion and waste accumulation
questions.explanation: As nutrients deplete and toxic waste products accumulate, growth rate slows until cell division balances cell death, giving a plateau in population size.

questions.question: The time required for a bacterial population to double in number during exponential growth is called the:
questions.explanation: Generation (doubling) time is the interval needed for a microbial population to double during the log phase; it varies widely between species and with growth conditions.

questions.question: Which method of measuring bacterial growth counts only living cells capable of forming colonies?
questions.explanation: The viable plate count method dilutes and plates a sample so that each living, colony-forming cell grows into a visible colony, allowing only living cells to be enumerated, unlike direct counts which include dead cells.

questions.question: Bacteria that grow best at temperatures between about 20°C and 45°C, including most human pathogens, are classified as:
questions.explanation: Mesophiles have an optimum growth temperature around 20-45°C, which includes normal human body temperature, explaining why most pathogens are mesophilic.

questions.question: Organisms that grow optimally at temperatures above 80°C, often found in hydrothermal vents, are called:
questions.explanation: Hyperthermophiles, many of which are archaea, have optimum growth temperatures above 80°C and thrive in extreme environments such as deep-sea hydrothermal vents.

questions.question: Most bacteria, described as neutrophiles, grow best within a pH range of approximately:
questions.explanation: Most bacteria are neutrophiles that grow optimally near neutral pH (about 6.5-7.5), in contrast to acidophiles (low pH) and alkaliphiles (high pH).

questions.question: Bacteria that require oxygen for growth and cannot grow without it are termed:
questions.explanation: Obligate aerobes depend entirely on aerobic respiration and molecular oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, and cannot survive in its absence.

questions.question: An organism that can grow either in the presence or absence of oxygen, using aerobic respiration when oxygen is available and fermentation or anaerobic respiration when it is not, is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Facultative anaerobes such as E. coli can switch metabolic strategies, preferring aerobic respiration when oxygen is present but surviving by fermentation when it is absent.

questions.question: Obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen mainly because they lack the enzymes needed to detoxify reactive oxygen species, particularly:
questions.explanation: Superoxide dismutase and catalase neutralise toxic superoxide radicals and hydrogen peroxide generated in the presence of oxygen; obligate anaerobes typically lack these enzymes.

questions.question: Microorganisms that require high salt concentrations for optimal growth are termed:
questions.explanation: Halophiles thrive in high-salinity environments such as salt lakes and require elevated salt concentrations to maintain osmotic balance and enzyme function.

questions.question: A protein catalyst that speeds up a biochemical reaction without itself being consumed is called a/an:
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins, that lower the activation energy of specific reactions and are regenerated unchanged at the end of the reaction.

questions.question: A non-protein organic molecule, such as NAD+ or FAD, that assists an enzyme in catalysing a reaction is called a:
questions.explanation: Coenzymes are small organic molecules (often derived from vitamins) that bind to enzymes and participate in catalysis, for example by transferring electrons or functional groups.

questions.question: In microbial metabolism, fermentation differs from aerobic respiration mainly in that fermentation:
options: Uses an organic molecule, rather than oxygen, as the final electron acceptor
Produces far more ATP per glucose molecule
Requires molecular oxygen as a substrate
questions.correct_answer: Uses an organic molecule, rather than oxygen, as the final electron acceptor
questions.explanation: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ by transferring electrons to an organic molecule (such as pyruvate, forming lactate or ethanol) rather than to oxygen, and yields far less ATP than respiration.

questions.question: Glycolysis, the central pathway that breaks down glucose to pyruvate, takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is a cytoplasmic (cytosolic) pathway in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, converting one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.

questions.question: Bacteria reproduce asexually most commonly by:
questions.explanation: Binary fission is the predominant mode of bacterial reproduction, in which a single cell replicates its chromosome and divides into two genetically identical daughter cells.

questions.question: Penicillin inhibits bacterial growth primarily by:
options: Blocking the cross-linking (transpeptidation) step of peptidoglycan synthesis
questions.correct_answer: Blocking the cross-linking (transpeptidation) step of peptidoglycan synthesis
questions.explanation: Penicillin and other beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit the transpeptidation reaction that cross-links peptidoglycan strands, weakening the cell wall and causing lysis.

questions.question: Protoplasts and spheroplasts, which are osmotically fragile bacterial forms lacking most or all of their cell wall, are typically produced experimentally using the enzyme:
questions.explanation: Lysozyme hydrolyses the beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds in peptidoglycan, digesting the cell wall and, under isotonic conditions, converting the cell into a wall-deficient protoplast or spheroplast.

questions.question: Archaeal cell walls differ from bacterial cell walls chiefly in that archaea:
options: Lack peptidoglycan, using pseudopeptidoglycan or other polymers instead
Always possess a thick peptidoglycan layer identical to Gram-positive bacteria
Have no cell wall or membrane at all
Use cellulose as their principal wall polymer
questions.correct_answer: Lack peptidoglycan, using pseudopeptidoglycan or other polymers instead
questions.explanation: True peptidoglycan is unique to bacteria; archaea have varied cell wall chemistries such as pseudopeptidoglycan, polysaccharides, or glycoproteins, and lack the beta-1,4 linkages targeted by lysozyme.

questions.question: Which nutritional group obtains energy from light but uses organic compounds, rather than CO2, as the carbon source?
questions.explanation: Photoheterotrophs, such as some purple non-sulfur bacteria, capture light energy but rely on organic molecules for carbon, combining photo- energy capture with heterotrophic carbon nutrition.

questions.question: During the death phase of a bacterial growth curve, the population declines because:
options: Cells die faster than new cells are produced, often following an exponential (logarithmic) decline
Cells stop producing toxic metabolic waste
questions.correct_answer: Cells die faster than new cells are produced, often following an exponential (logarithmic) decline
questions.explanation: In the death phase, accumulated toxic products and exhausted nutrients cause cells to die at a rate exceeding new cell formation, often in an exponential pattern, though some resistant cells may persist.
